title: Cholesterol Calculator: Total/LDL/HDL 2026 | Hacé Cuentas
description: Cholesterol calculator: check if your Total (<200), LDL (<100), and HDL (>60) levels are in the healthy range. Instant, evidence-based results.
intro:
Understanding your cholesterol numbers is one of the most actionable steps you can take for long-term cardiovascular health — yet most people receive their lab results without any real explanation of what those numbers mean in practice. This calculator closes that gap by instantly comparing your Total Cholesterol, LDL, and HDL values against the clinically established reference ranges used by major health organizations, including the American Heart Association (AHA), the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI), and the World Health Organization (WHO).

Cholesterol is a waxy, fat-like substance found in every cell of your body. It's essential for producing hormones, vitamin D, and the bile acids that help digest food. The problem isn't cholesterol itself — it's the balance between its forms. LDL (low-density lipoprotein), often called 'bad' cholesterol, tends to deposit in arterial walls, forming plaques that narrow blood vessels and raise the risk of heart attack and stroke. HDL (high-density lipoprotein), the 'good' cholesterol, acts as a reverse transporter, pulling excess cholesterol from the arteries and delivering it to the liver for disposal. Total cholesterol is simply the sum of all cholesterol fractions in your blood.

The reference thresholds used in this calculator — Total Cholesterol below 200 mg/dL, LDL below 100 mg/dL, and HDL above 60 mg/dL (above 40 mg/dL for men, above 50 mg/dL for women) — are derived from decades of large-scale epidemiological research, including the landmark Framingham Heart Study and the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES). These are not arbitrary cutoffs: each threshold corresponds to a statistically meaningful inflection point in cardiovascular event rates across diverse populations.

What makes this tool unique is not just the instant color-coded feedback on each value, but the context it provides around gender-specific HDL targets, borderline ranges, and the interaction between different cholesterol fractions. A total cholesterol of 210 mg/dL reads very differently if your HDL is 75 mg/dL versus 38 mg/dL — and this calculator helps you see that nuance immediately.

Important: this tool is designed for educational and self-monitoring purposes. Cholesterol management is highly individualized — your physician will factor in your age, family history, blood pressure, smoking status, diabetes, and existing cardiovascular disease before recommending any treatment. Use these results as a starting point for an informed conversation with your healthcare provider, not as a substitute for one.

explanation:
**Healthy cholesterol values** come from large population studies (NHANES, WHO, CDC). They vary by age, sex, ethnicity, and region. They're guidelines; your personal medical history always takes priority.

## How It's Calculated

Target ranges: Total <200, LDL <100, HDL >60 (men >40, women >50).

This calculator applies the formula with your input values, checks typical ranges, and alerts you to any unusual readings.

## Normal Reference Ranges

| Parameter | Normal Range (Adults) |
|---|---|
| Blood Pressure | <120/80 mmHg |
| Resting Heart Rate | 60-100 bpm |
| Temperature | 36.1-37.2°C |
| Oxygen Saturation (SpO2) | 95-100% |
| Fasting Glucose | 70-100 mg/dL |
| HbA1c | <5.7% |
| Total Cholesterol | <200 mg/dL |
| LDL Cholesterol | <100 mg/dL |
| HDL Cholesterol | >40 (men) / >50 (women) |

## Important Notes

This calculation is for guidance only. For critical decisions (medical, financial, legal), consult a qualified healthcare professional. Values are current as of 2026 and reviewed periodically.

faq.q: What do the reference ranges in this calculator actually mean, and where do they come from?
faq.a: The thresholds used — Total Cholesterol below 200 mg/dL, LDL below 100 mg/dL, HDL above 60 mg/dL (men above 40, women above 50) — are based on decades of cardiovascular epidemiology, most importantly the Framingham Heart Study, NHANES population surveys, and clinical guidelines published by the American Heart Association (AHA) and the American College of Cardiology (ACC). These cutoffs represent statistically validated inflection points where cardiovascular event risk begins to rise meaningfully. They are not absolute guarantees: a person with LDL of 105 mg/dL but excellent HDL, low blood pressure, and no family history may carry less risk than someone with LDL of 95 mg/dL but multiple additional risk factors. Think of these ranges as a starting benchmark, not a final verdict.

faq.q: What is the difference between fasting and non-fasting cholesterol tests?
faq.a: Total cholesterol and HDL are relatively stable regardless of whether you've eaten recently, so non-fasting measurements are reasonably accurate for those values. LDL, however, is traditionally calculated using the Friedewald equation (LDL = Total − HDL − Triglycerides/5), which requires a fasting triglyceride measurement for accuracy. Eating before the test can temporarily spike triglycerides, distorting the LDL calculation. Modern labs increasingly use direct LDL assays that are less affected by fasting status, but your doctor will typically still request an 8–12 hour fast for a comprehensive lipid panel. If your lab result states 'non-fasting,' ask whether a fasting test is warranted for a more precise LDL figure.

faq.q: Why is HDL called 'good' cholesterol — and can it ever be too high?
faq.a: HDL earns its 'good' reputation through reverse cholesterol transport: it picks up excess cholesterol from peripheral tissues, including arterial plaques, and shuttles it back to the liver for breakdown and excretion. Higher HDL has historically been associated with lower cardiovascular risk. However, recent research, including large Mendelian randomization studies, suggests that extremely high HDL (above 100 mg/dL) does not continue to provide protective benefits and may in some cases be associated with increased mortality, possibly due to dysfunctional HDL particles. For most people, HDL between 60 and 90 mg/dL represents a healthy target range. Very high HDL without a clear dietary or genetic cause should be discussed with a physician.

faq.q: How do triglycerides relate to the values in this calculator?
faq.a: Triglycerides are a separate lipid measured in a full lipid panel and are not directly entered into this calculator, but they interact critically with your cholesterol profile. High triglycerides (above 150 mg/dL) often accompany low HDL and small, dense LDL particles — a pattern called atherogenic dyslipidemia that significantly elevates cardiovascular risk even when total LDL appears acceptable. Elevated triglycerides are often linked to excess sugar intake, refined carbohydrates, alcohol, obesity, insulin resistance, and certain medications. If your Total and LDL look fine but you know your triglycerides are high, consider discussing a complete metabolic and cardiovascular risk assessment with your doctor, not just individual lipid values.

faq.q: What is the non-HDL cholesterol metric, and why do some doctors use it instead of LDL?
faq.a: Non-HDL cholesterol equals Total Cholesterol minus HDL. It captures all atherogenic (artery-clogging) lipoprotein particles in a single number, including LDL, VLDL, IDL, and Lp(a) — giving a broader picture of cardiovascular risk than LDL alone. This is particularly useful for patients with high triglycerides, where the traditional Friedewald LDL calculation becomes unreliable. The optimal non-HDL target is generally below 130 mg/dL (i.e., 30 mg/dL above the LDL target). You can calculate it yourself: if your Total is 190 mg/dL and HDL is 55 mg/dL, your non-HDL is 135 mg/dL — slightly above optimal. Some current ACC/AHA guidelines now recommend non-HDL as a primary treatment target alongside LDL.

faq.q: Do cholesterol targets change with age, and should older adults aim for the same numbers?
faq.a: Cholesterol management guidelines do evolve with age, though not simply in one direction. In adults under 40, even mildly elevated LDL deserves attention because long-term arterial exposure accumulates over decades. In adults 40–75, guidelines increasingly recommend using the 10-year cardiovascular risk score (such as the Pooled Cohort Equations) to determine whether statin therapy is appropriate, rather than treating LDL in isolation. In adults over 75, the evidence for aggressive lipid-lowering is more nuanced — shared decision-making between patient and physician becomes especially important. For older adults already on statins, abrupt discontinuation can be harmful. The reference ranges in this calculator reflect general population targets; individualized goals must account for age and overall risk profile.

faq.q: How much can lifestyle changes realistically lower LDL and raise HDL?
faq.a: Lifestyle modifications can produce meaningful but variable results. Dietary changes — particularly reducing saturated fat (found in red meat, butter, and full-fat dairy) and replacing it with unsaturated fats (olive oil, nuts, avocado) — can lower LDL by 10–20% in compliant individuals. Adding soluble fiber (oats, legumes, psyllium) contributes an additional 5–10% reduction. Regular aerobic exercise (at least 150 minutes per week of moderate-intensity activity) is one of the few evidence-based ways to raise HDL, typically by 3–6 mg/dL. Weight loss of 5–10% of body weight can improve all lipid parameters. Smoking cessation raises HDL. Combined, these measures can sometimes eliminate the need for medication in borderline cases — but they require consistency and usually take 3–6 months to show measurable laboratory impact.

faq.q: What is the LDL-C versus LDL-P distinction, and does it matter?
faq.a: Most standard lipid panels measure LDL cholesterol concentration (LDL-C) — the amount of cholesterol carried by LDL particles. However, emerging evidence suggests that LDL particle number (LDL-P), measured by advanced lipoprotein testing like NMR spectroscopy or apolipoprotein B (ApoB) levels, may better predict cardiovascular risk. This is because small, dense LDL particles carry less cholesterol per particle but are more atherogenic — meaning someone can have a 'normal' LDL-C of 98 mg/dL but a high LDL-P if their particles are small and numerous. ApoB testing (one ApoB molecule per atherogenic particle) is an affordable proxy for LDL-P and is increasingly recommended by some cardiology guidelines for patients with metabolic syndrome, diabetes, or discordance between LDL-C and non-HDL cholesterol.

faq.q: Can genetic conditions cause abnormal cholesterol levels even in healthy, fit individuals?
faq.a: Yes. Familial Hypercholesterolemia (FH) is the most common serious genetic lipid disorder, affecting approximately 1 in 250 people worldwide. It is caused by mutations in the LDL receptor gene, causing LDL to remain elevated (often above 190 mg/dL) regardless of diet or exercise. Heterozygous FH often goes undiagnosed for years because affected individuals may appear healthy and physically fit. Other genetic conditions, such as familial combined hyperlipidemia, sitosterolemia, and polygenic hypercholesterolemia, can also cause persistent dyslipidemia. If your LDL is consistently above 190 mg/dL despite healthy lifestyle habits, or if close relatives had premature heart disease (before age 55 in men, before 65 in women), genetic testing and specialized evaluation are strongly recommended.

faq.q: How do statins work, and are there alternatives if I can't tolerate them?
faq.a: Statins (atorvastatin, rosuvastatin, simvastatin, etc.) inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, the enzyme that controls cholesterol synthesis in the liver. By reducing liver cholesterol production, they upregulate LDL receptors, which then pull more LDL out of the bloodstream — reducing LDL by 30–60% depending on the drug and dose. Statins also have modest pleiotropic (anti-inflammatory, plaque-stabilizing) effects beyond lipid lowering. For patients who experience statin-related muscle pain (myalgia), alternatives include ezetimibe (which blocks intestinal cholesterol absorption and can lower LDL by 15–25%), PCSK9 inhibitors (injectable biologics that can cut LDL by 50–60%, approved for high-risk patients), bempedoic acid, and bile acid sequestrants. Your physician will weigh efficacy, tolerability, cost, and your specific risk profile when choosing an approach.

faq.q: Is it possible to have cardiovascular disease with 'normal' cholesterol levels?
faq.a: Yes, and this is one of the most important nuances in cardiovascular medicine. A significant proportion of people who suffer heart attacks have total cholesterol below 200 mg/dL at the time of the event. This is because LDL-C is only one of many cardiovascular risk factors — inflammation (measured by high-sensitivity CRP), elevated Lp(a), hypertension, smoking, diabetes, insulin resistance, sleep apnea, psychosocial stress, and physical inactivity all contribute independently. Additionally, as discussed above, LDL particle quality matters as much as quantity. A coronary calcium score (CAC) via CT scan, for example, can detect subclinical atherosclerosis even in people with apparently normal lipid panels. 'Normal' cholesterol is reassuring but not a guarantee — comprehensive cardiovascular risk assessment goes well beyond a single lipid panel.

faq.q: How should I interpret my results if my values fall in the 'borderline' range?
faq.a: Borderline values — for example, Total Cholesterol between 200–239 mg/dL, LDL between 100–129 mg/dL, or HDL between 40–59 mg/dL — are not automatically alarming, but they warrant attention and context. The significance of borderline results depends heavily on your other cardiovascular risk factors: age (risk increases significantly after 45 in men and 55 in women), sex, smoking status, blood pressure, family history, diabetes status, and prior cardiovascular events. For a 35-year-old non-smoking woman with no family history, a Total Cholesterol of 210 mg/dL may require only lifestyle monitoring. For a 58-year-old man with hypertension and a diabetic parent, the same value may prompt immediate medication discussion. The American Heart Association offers a free 10-year ASCVD risk calculator that incorporates all these factors — using it alongside your cholesterol results gives a much more complete picture than lipid values alone.
